# Changelog

Every **resolved issue** of Exudyn, newest first, with the version it produced. The micro version *is* the count of closed issues, so each line below is one version number: 1.10.160 is the 160th issue closed in release 1.10. An issue that was closed without being resolved is in no list: it changed nothing - which is why a release can span more version numbers than it has lines here.

Every entry carries the **type** of the issue, then its **priority** and its **effort** as badges (`LOW EFF` is within 2 hours, `MEDIUM EFF` is within 16 hours, `HIGH EFF` is within 40 hours, `HUGE EFF` is above 40 hours), then who raised it and who resolved it - both omitted when that was Johannes Gerstmayr (JG).

This file is generated; it is written by the tracker whenever an issue closes.

**Only the current release is below.** The issues resolved before it, in the same form, are in the {ref}`issue tracker <sec-issuetracker>` of the documentation, which also lists the open issues and the known bugs; the table that follows is the whole history at a glance.

## Version 1.13 - Newborn (current)

- **1.13.591** `EXTENSION` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` The raytracer runs with several threads while a solver runs, from the renderer thread (#3438)
  - description: The raytracer can be started from the main thread and from the renderer thread; the one TaskManager is global, so while a solver uses the threads the raytracer falls back to one thread, and a raytracer started in the renderer thread during a solve crashes. The raytracer shall run in parallel to the solver with threads of its own.
  - **notes:** The raytracer renders on threads of its own (visualizationSettings.raytracer.numberOfThreads), independent of the threads of the solvers: it runs in parallel also while a solver runs, from a user function or from the renderer thread; the speed is unchanged. The persistent threads of exudyn.special.solver.StartPersistentThreads are no longer used by the raytracer. Test model raytracerDuringSolveTest.py.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 14:04**, date raised: 2026-11-11
- **1.13.589** `IMPROVEMENT` `HIGH EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` ObjectFFRF: analytic Jacobian instead of the numerical one (#3447)
  - description: ObjectFFRF computes its ODE2 Jacobian numerically: one evaluation of the element per coordinate and a dense block of all coordinates. With the mass matrix as triplets (\#2183) it is the largest cost of the element on larger meshes (7.9 s of 24 s for 1525 nodes and 20 steps). An analytic Jacobian - the stiffness and damping matrices as stored triplets plus the coupling terms of the floating frame, as for ObjectFFRFreducedOrder - returned as sparse triplets.
  - **notes:** ObjectFFRF computes its ODE2 Jacobian as sparse triplets - stiffness, damping and the quadratic velocity terms by the mesh coordinates analytic, by the rotation parameters by local differences -, on Euler parameters and Tait-Bryan angles without a forceUserFunction: 550 times faster than the numerical Jacobian at 1525 nodes; ObjectFFRF.numericalJacobian = True lets the system differentiate it as before
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 08:58**, date raised: 2026-11-12
- **1.13.588** `IMPROVEMENT` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Clean up the interface between the superelement markers and the superelements (#3450)
  - description: MarkerSuperElementPosition and MarkerSuperElementRigid compute their sums over the mesh nodes through a set of functions of the superelements (GetMeshNodeLocalPosition, GetMeshNodePosition, ...); the code is cleaned up and the interface adapted, as the base of the precomputed interface sums (\#2184).
  - **notes:** the interface between the superelement markers and the superelements: what a marker needs of its mesh nodes is computed by the superelement at Assemble; a changed weightingFactors takes effect without a new Assemble; the position of MarkerSuperElementPosition with weights that do not sum up to 1 follows the floating frame like that of MarkerSuperElementRigid
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 08:32**, date raised: 2026-11-12
- **1.13.587** `EXTENSION` `MEDIUM EFF` `resolved by: Claude-JG` MarkerSuperElementRigid (#2184)
  - description: highly improve efficiency for larger number of nodes by adding according precomputed transformations
  - **notes:** MarkerSuperElementPosition and MarkerSuperElementRigid on ObjectFFRFreducedOrder compute their sums over the mesh nodes from the weighted modes, formed once at Assemble (ObjectFFRFreducedOrder.precomputeMarkerModes, default True; False computes them from the mesh nodes): 30-170 times faster for interfaces of 135-620 nodes
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 08:32**, date raised: 2026-01-04
- **1.13.586** `CHANGE` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` ObjectFFRF.sparseMassMatrix replaces exudyn.special.solver.superElementSparseMassMatrix (#3449)
  - description: The switch between the sparse and the dense mass matrix of ObjectFFRF (\#2183) belongs to the object, as a parameter that is kept with the model, not to exudyn.special.
  - **notes:** ObjectFFRF.sparseMassMatrix (default True) switches between the mass matrix as sparse triplets and the dense matrix; it replaces exu.special.solver.superElementSparseMassMatrix
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 07:46**, date raised: 2026-11-12
- **1.13.585** `EXTENSION` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` simulationSettings.linearSolver.dropThreshold: leave out the near-zero entries of the sparse Newton Jacobian (#3448)
  - description: The sparse Newton Jacobian keeps every entry that is not exactly zero. In chains of rigid bodies and in contact models, 14-55 % of the nonzeros are smaller than 1e-12 times the largest entry of their row and of their column: round-off of rotations and of numerical derivatives, which cost fill-in in the factorization. A relative threshold leaves them out in GeneralMatrixEigenSparse::FinalizeMatrix, for the Newton Jacobian only; the solution is unchanged, as the residual is exact.
  - **notes:** simulationSettings.linearSolver.dropThreshold: the sparse Newton Jacobian leaves out the entries at most dropThreshold times the smaller of the largest magnitudes of their row and their column (round-off of rotations and numerical derivatives); default 0, only exact zeros; with 1e-12 a chain of rigid body spring-dampers with full Newton is 17 % faster, a chain of revolute joints 13 % slower, the results the same
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 07:46**, date raised: 2026-11-12

- **1.13.578** `CHANGE` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` raytracer.numberOfThreads = 0 selects the number of logical processors, and is the default (#3445)
  - description: The default visualizationSettings.raytracer.numberOfThreads was 8; since the raytracer balances its tiles dynamically (\#3439) it scales up to the number of logical processors (0.664 s with 8 against 0.37 s with 32 threads on 16 cores / 32 logical processors). The value 0 selects the number of logical processors (std::thread::hardware\_concurrency) and is the new default; a positive value is used as before.
  - **notes:** visualizationSettings.raytracer.numberOfThreads = 0, the new default, uses the number of logical processors of the computer; the raytracer balances its tiles over them.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-12 01:14**, date raised: 2026-11-12

- **1.13.575** `IMPROVEMENT` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` SparseLU solves with the rows of its factors instead of the supernodal solve of Eigen (#3441)
  - description: After a factorization of EigenSparse (COLAMD), the factors L and U are copied into rows and the forward and backward substitution run on them, as with special.solver.parallelSubstitution: there the serial substitution by rows was 1.6-2.8 times faster than the supernodal solve of Eigen on chains (small supernodes, vector copies); for modified Newton with many solves per factorization; the copy costs about 0.3 ms per factorization of 13000 unknowns. Measured against the solve of today on the performance and test models with sparse solvers.
  - **notes:** EigenSparse solves with the rows of the factors of SparseLU instead of the supernodal solve of Eigen: the solves are about twice as fast, the performance models with sparse solvers 2.4 % and the test models 2.8 % faster in total, up to 18 %; exu.special.solver.sparseSolveByRows = False switches back. Results change by round-off.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-11 22:33**, date raised: 2026-11-11
- **1.13.574** `CHECK` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Study the scaling of the raytracer with the number of threads (#3439)
  - description: The raytracer reaches its best speed only with 64-128 threads on a machine with 16 cores, although each thread gets small portions of work. Measure and explain the scaling (the static split of tasks without load balancing, the tiles per thread, the spinning workers, the memory access) and what it tells about the parallel loops of Exudyn in general.
  - **notes:** The raytracer always balances its tiles dynamically over its threads, whatever load balancing the last solver used; without it each thread rendered a fixed band of the image, and the raytracer needed 64-128 threads on 16 cores for its best time; now it reaches it with about the number of logical processors (0.37 s on 32 threads for the scene of raytracerNOGLFWtest.py at 1200 x 1000, 12.6 times faster than one thread).
  - date resolved: **2026-11-11 22:33**, date raised: 2026-11-11

- **1.13.572** `EXTENSION` `HIGH EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` A parallel forward and backward substitution of the sparse solver with a nested-dissection ordering (#3432)
  - description: With modified Newton and a Jacobian that hardly changes, the back-substitution is done far more often than the factorization; with the minimum-degree or COLAMD orderings of today, chains have 2-7 unknowns per level of the triangular solves, but a nested-dissection ordering gives speedup bounds of 18-60 at about twice the fill; an ordering by nested dissection (without METIS), the factors in a plain format after each factorization and the substitution by subtrees of the elimination tree on Exudyn's threads, measured against the serial solve of SparseLU (design docs/dev/design/sparseSolvers.md section 4).
  - **notes:** exu.special.solver.parallelSubstitution (experimental, default False): EigenSparse factorizes with a nested-dissection ordering on the Jacobian pattern and the coordinates of each object, and the forward and backward substitution run by the subtrees of the ordering on the threads; the solves are 1.8-4.4 times faster than with SparseLU on 8 threads, the factorization slower on several threads; modified Newton on large chains 9-13 % faster in total, small systems and full Newton slower; parallelSubstitutionPivotThreshold and parallelSubstitutionSerial in exu.special.solver.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-11 21:31**, date raised: 2026-11-11
- **1.13.571** `CHECK` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` What the systems of one SystemContainer share, before they are solved in parallel (#3440)
  - description: A pre-analysis for \#3433: the global and static state, the GIL, the output, the errors, the files and the renderer interplay that two solvers on threads of their own would share, classified as to be made per system or locked, safe, or unclear, with the hardest obstacles.
  - **notes:** Pre-analysis of solving the systems of one SystemContainer in parallel (docs/dev/design/systemContainerParallel.md): the solve does not release the GIL today; the shared state to be made per solver or locked (task manager, thread ids, timers, output, errors, renderer queues, file names), the safe parts and the main obstacles.

- **1.13.570** `EXTENSION` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Persistent worker threads of the TaskManager, started by exudyn.special.solver, sleeping between solves (#3437)
  - description: Every solver with numberOfThreads \> 1 starts and stops its worker threads; for many runs of small systems this costs. A function of exudyn.special.solver starts a number of workers that stay, sleeping on a condition variable while no solver uses them; a solver whose simulationSettings.parallel.numberOfThreads agrees uses them, one that disagrees uses its own number for that solve and writes a message (simulationSettings wins).
  - **notes:** exu.special.solver.StartPersistentThreads(n) starts n threads that stay, sleeping while no computation uses them; every solver with parallel.numberOfThreads = n uses them instead of starting and stopping threads of its own, which saves 0.2-0.8 ms per solve; a solver with another number of threads uses that number for its run, with a warning; StopPersistentThreads() and PersistentThreads() stop and count them; the raytracer uses them alike.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-11 20:32**, date raised: 2026-11-11

- **1.13.566** `EXTENSION` `HIGH EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` LinearSolverType.PardisoMKL: Intel MKL PARDISO loaded at run time from the Python environment, with a residual check and the fallback to SparseLU (#3431)
  - description: A sparse linear solver type that uses MKL PARDISO when the user has installed MKL (pip or conda); the C++ loads mkl\_rt at run time (no build dependency, nothing in the wheel), passes Eigen's compressed matrix without a copy, checks the residual after the first factorization of a pattern and periodically, falls back to SparseLU with a warning, and has its expert settings in exudyn.special.solver; exudyn.special.solver.PardisoInfo() tells whether MKL was found (design docs/dev/design/sparseSolvers.md section 2).
  - **notes:** LinearSolverType.PardisoMKL (experimental): Intel MKL PARDISO, which the user installs into the Python environment (pip install mkl), loaded at run time - nothing changes without it; the residual is checked after the factorizations, a failure continues with SparseLU and a warning; exudyn.special.solver.PardisoInfo() tells whether MKL is found, and exudyn.special.solver holds its settings; faster than EigenSparse for full Newton on large systems with several threads.

- **1.13.565** `CHECK` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Study the failures of MKL PARDISO on the Jacobians of Exudyn: the classes of models and the settings for which it is reliable (#3430)
  - description: Jacobians exported from ODE models, index-3 and index-2 constrained models and the extreme chain of 1000 rigid bodies on revolute joints, solved by MKL PARDISO through ctypes with the settings varied (two-level factorization, ordering, matching and scaling, pivot perturbation, refinement, numerical noise dropped, the transposed CSC hand-over, threads); the result decides the default parameters of the solver type and for which classes it is recommended (design docs/dev/design/sparseSolvers.md section 3).
  - **notes:** Studied why MKL PARDISO failed on Exudyn's Jacobians: the METIS ordering with the parallel or two-level factorization; the minimum degree ordering with the one-level factorization solves all 18 studied Jacobians (ODE, index 3, index 2, up to 13000 unknowns) on 1-16 threads to the accuracy of SuperLU; these are the defaults of LinearSolverType.PardisoMKL.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-11 17:16**, date raised: 2026-11-11
- **1.13.564** `IMPROVEMENT` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` The threads during the sparse factorization: Exudyn's workers spin while the factorization runs, and cannot be given to an external solver (#3428)
  - description: The workers of ExuThreading::TaskManager wait for jobs by spinning with yield, also during the factorization of the system Jacobian, which is serial in Eigen; SuspendWorkers and ResumeWorkers are empty stubs. A multi-threaded external solver (MKL PARDISO with OpenMP or TBB threads) would compete with them for the cores, and MKL cannot use Exudyn's threads. Options (docs/dev/design/sparseSolvers.md section 5): the workers sleep on a condition variable during a factorization (SuspendWorkers/ResumeWorkers implemented, the wake-up measured); and models of independent subsystems factorized and solved per connected component in a ParallelFor on Exudyn's own threads, which also parallelizes the back-substitution where a level-scheduled solve cannot (chains have about 3 unknowns per level).
  - **notes:** With several threads, exudyn.special.solver.suspendWorkersDuringFactorization (default False) lets the worker threads sleep on a condition variable while a sparse matrix of at least suspendWorkersMinimumSize unknowns is factorized, instead of spinning; full Newton on 8 threads becomes 12-14 % faster with a third of the CPU time. Factorizing independent subsystems on Exudyn's threads is not done.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-11 17:16**, date raised: 2026-11-11

- **1.13.561** `CHECK` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Design of a sparse solver by MKL PARDISO loaded at run time, evaluation of its failures and of the back-substitution (#3427)
  - description: MKL PARDISO factorizes Exudyn's sparse Jacobians 2.5-24 times faster than Eigen's SparseLU when its analysis is kept, but returned wrong solutions or failed on index-3 constrained chains (linalgBenchmark.md section 3.9). Design, before an implementation: MKL installed by the user (pip or conda) and loaded by the C++ at run time - no build dependency, no MKL in the wheel; the solver type, its settings, the hand-over of Eigen's compressed matrix without a copy, the residual check after a factorization with a fallback to SparseLU; a study of the causes of the failures (format, scaling, conditioning, numerical noise in the Jacobian, saddle-point pivots, settings); whether the serial back-substitution can be parallelized. Design note docs/dev/design/sparseSolvers.md.
  - **notes:** Designed and evaluated (docs/dev/design/sparseSolvers.md), Exudyn unchanged: a solver type PardisoMKL whose MKL the user installs (pip or conda) and the C++ loads at run time - no build dependency, nothing in the wheel - with Eigen's compressed matrix passed without a copy, a residual check after the factorization and a fallback to SparseLU; a study of the failures of PARDISO (half of the stored Jacobian entries are numerical noise, conditions up to 2e11, equilibration did not help); the back-substitution of chain-like systems has about 3 unknowns per level and is not parallelized by levels - independent subsystems solved on Exudyn's threads instead.

  - description: ObjectFFRFinterface.AddObjectFFRF of exudyn.FEM documents gravity as the gravity vector applied to the body, stores it in self.gravity and never applies it (the code in UFforceFFRF is commented out). Gravity on an ObjectFFRF needs the rotational part -G^T rf~^T A\_bd^T M Phi\_t g of Zwoelfer and Gerstmayr 2019, Eq. (14.88), which the forceVector of ObjectFFRF does not give (objectFFRFforceVectorTest.py, \#591); nodal loads at the mesh nodes give it exactly. Either apply it, e.g. by a LoadMassProportional or by nodal loads, or remove the argument.
  - **notes:** ObjectFFRFinterface.AddObjectFFRF applies gravity as a LoadMassProportional on a MarkerBodyMass; that load acts on all coordinates of an ObjectFFRF, with the deformed positions, and the center of mass of ObjectFFRF is computed from the reference positions

- **1.13.526** `CHANGE` `HIGH EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` joints and their Jacobians on homogeneous transformations (#2884)
  - description: The constraint equations of the joints become functions of the relative transformation H0^-1 H1 of the two marker frames, and their Jacobians follow systematically from the relative twist - one implementation for JointGeneric, JointRevoluteZ, JointPrismaticX, the 2D joints and the rolling disc instead of one each. Successor of \#2745 (the marker interface of RG14.2). revision2026b step RG14.3
  - **notes:** ObjectJointGeneric, ObjectJointRevoluteZ and ObjectJointPrismaticX compute their equations with one implementation on the relative frame of their joint frames, with analytic derivatives instead of automatic differentiation; the velocity level is their derivative times the velocities of the markers. Their reaction forces take half the time, a chain of revolute joints with modified Newton about 20 % less in all; the velocity level of the alternative constraints of ObjectJointGeneric is now the time derivative of these constraints.

- **1.13.523** `IMPROVEMENT` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` A trajectory along a planned path which rounds its corners and keeps the limits of the joints (#3397)
  - description: TrajectoryFromPath blended point-to-point profiles: each one accelerated and decelerated, so that the motion along a path of many waypoints braked and accelerated often (the wall scene of pathPlanningUR5.py stopped seven times), the blending could not be adjusted, and the blend could exceed the acceleration limits. Decided: ProfileJointPath, straight edges whose corners are rounded by curves of an adjustable size (blendRadius), with the largest velocity along the path that the velocity and acceleration limits of the joints allow; TrajectoryFromPath uses it and reduces the rounding where the check finds a collision.
  - **notes:** ProfileJointPath moves along a path of waypoints in joint space with corners rounded by curves of an adjustable size (blendRadius), as fast as the velocity and acceleration limits of the joints allow and without stopping at the waypoints; TrajectoryFromPath uses it and reduces the rounding where it would collide.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-10 00:44**, date raised: 2026-11-10

  - description: An icosahedron dropped flat onto a box with ObjectContactConvexConvex makes the solver fail at the minimum step size when it touches: all 12 points are over the face of the box, the 8 deepest are kept, and points of equal height take turns among the kept ones from one Newton iteration to the next; as the kept points are given to the data blocks in the order of their ids, the 3 points in contact move to other blocks, and the contact state of the data never settles. - **1.13.456** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `HIGH` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` ObjectJournalBearing pushes the journal out when it turns the other way about the bearing axis (#3345)
  - description: The film forces of ObjectJournalBearing (infinitely short and long bearing after Flores et al. 2009) hold for a positive w = omega - 2 gammaDot, the film in the converging gap in the direction of rotation; with a negative w, a journal turning the other way about the axis of marker 1, the radial force pushes the journal outwards and the tangential force acts on the wrong side: a rotor of contactPrimitivesShowcase.py turning at -50 rad/s about the axis drifts to the clearance instead of floating at its equilibrium. Decided: for a negative w the forces of the mirrored bearing - w by its magnitude, the tangential direction reversed; a test of both directions of rotation in journalBearingTest.py.

- **1.13.455** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `HIGH` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` EPA returns a normal that is not converged when it stops early: the faces of a resting polytope are missed (#3346)
  - description: Since \#3338 the expanding polytope algorithm stops when a new point would turn a face over; the face it stops at is then not a face of the Minkowski difference, and its normal is off by up to 0.01 rad: in 2 of 5000 poses of an icosahedron resting on a face on a box (contactPrimitivesShowcase.py). ObjectContactConvexConvex takes the face manifold only for a normal within 1e-6 of a face normal, so it switches between the face points and one closest point from one Newton iteration to the next, and the discontinuous iteration fails at the minimum step size. Decided: EPA says whether it converged; if not, the penetration is refined as for the cylinders, by moving shape 1 out along the normal until the separated distance gives a face of the difference; resting poses of an icosahedron in convexConvexContactTest.py.
  - **notes:** Where the expanding polytope algorithm stops before it converges, the penetration of two convex shapes is refined: a polytope resting on a face, as an icosahedron on a box with ObjectContactConvexConvex, keeps the normal of the face, which the contact needs for its points.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-07 22:11**, date raised: 2026-11-07

- **1.13.452** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `HIGH` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` EPA loses the origin where two convex shapes touch on faces: a resting cube sinks into a box (#3338)
  - description: A cube resting flat on a box with ObjectContactConvexConvex (contactPrimitivesShowcase.py) sinks 2 cm into it after 0.47 s and jumps: in about 2 percent of the poses near rest, the expanding polytope algorithm adds points of tiny height on the nearly flat side of the Minkowski difference until a thin face turns over, the origin lies outside the polytope, and the distance is returned as -0 with the normal of the opposite side; the iteration limit of 128 is reached, which also makes the contact slow. Decided: EPA starts from the tetrahedron of GJK, which contains the origin, refuses a point that is a vertex already and, while expanding, a face that has the origin outside; a test of resting poses in convexConvexContactTest.py.
  - **notes:** A convex shape resting on a face of another, as a cube on a box with ObjectContactConvexConvex, was in some poses pushed into it: the penetration was returned as 0 with the normal of the opposite side. The expanding polytope algorithm keeps the origin inside its polytope; such contacts are also faster.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-07 21:03**, date raised: 2026-11-07

- **1.13.429** `DOCU` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` The solver study: zero multipliers as a group, the efficiency figure split into constant and automatic steps (#3311)
  - description: The algebraic coordinates of rigidBodySpringDampers are the multipliers of the Euler parameter constraints, which are zero in the exact solution (G theta = 0: neither the mass matrix nor the forces act along the parameters); their reference is 0 to 1e-12, so the relative error of the figure is noise divided by 1e-14 (1 to 1e4).   - description: The rotation of a stage was the composition of the start of the step with the increment h sum\_j A\_ij omega\_j, the formula of the other coordinates; the rotation vector of the increment differs from it by terms of h^2, so LobattoIIIA4, LobattoIIIC4GGL and Radau3 converged with order 2 on the spatial slider crank of modelLibrary.py with NodeRigidBodyRotVecLG (4, 4, 3 with Euler parameters). - **1.13.403** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `HIGH` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` the initial accelerations of the implicit solvers are wrong for Euler parameters and Lie group nodes with initial velocities (#3289)
  - description: The initial accelerations solve \[M C\_q^T; C\_q 0\] \[a; lambda\] = \[f; -(C\_q v)\_q v\]. With Euler parameter nodes C\_q v left out the part of C\_q along the Euler parameters, which the rows of the matrix contain since \#3201; with Lie group nodes (C\_q v)\_q was differentiated by adding to the rotation vector, while the velocities are angular velocities. On a body on a spherical joint away from its center, spinning, the accelerations were wrong by up to 1 (of 5); with Rxyz nodes they were right. Generalized-alpha starts from them, LobattoIIIA4 uses them in its first stage, which limited it to order 2 on the spatial slider crank of modelLibrary.py. Decided: (C\_q v)\_q v as the central difference of C\_q v along the motion - the positions moved by +-eps v, Lie group nodes by the composition, C\_q with its part along the Euler parameters; revision2026c step RG20.7.4.
  - **notes:** The term (C\_q v)\_q v of the initial accelerations is the central difference of fourth order of C\_q v along the motion: the positions moved by +-eps v and +-2 eps v, the rotation of Lie group nodes by the composition, C\_q v with its part along the Euler parameters (CSystem::ComputeConstraintVelocityTerm, dense and sparse). The initial accelerations of Euler parameters and Lie group nodes with initial velocities were wrong, by up to a quarter on the spatial slider crank; generalized-alpha and LobattoIIIA4 start from them. initialAccelerationsTest.py: a rigid body on a spherical joint with three node types.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-06 11:17**, date raised: 2026-11-06
- **1.13.402** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `NORMAL` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` The composition of rotation vectors loses rotation increments below 1e-8 rad; Lie group nodes in the implicit Runge-Kutta solvers (#3288)
  - description: EXUlie::CompositionRotationVector (and CompositionRuleForRotationVectors of lieGroupBasics.py) takes the composed angle from x = cos(w/2) by sqrt(1 - x^2): for w below about 1e-8 rad x rounds to 1 and the angle to 0, so small rotation increments are quantized. With NodeRigidBodyRotVecLG this is the floor of 2e-10 at which the Newton iteration of LobattoIIIA4 and Radau3 stalls at small steps (the slider crank at h = 6.25e-5 fails); generalized-alpha composes with the same function. Decided (revision2026c step RG20.7.2): sin(w/2) from the vector part of the quaternion product, \|rho\|/2, which is the same in exact arithmetic and accurate for small angles; the tangent operator T(Delta) in the stage Jacobian of the implicit Runge-Kutta solvers, as generalized-alpha with lieGroupAddTangentOperator; a check of the stage Jacobian against finite differences at verbose level 4; the order of the rotations measured.
  - **notes:** EXUlie::CompositionRotationVector and lieGroupBasics.CompositionRuleForRotationVectors take the composed angle as 2 atan2(\|rho\|/2, x) from the quaternion product, instead of from x = cos(w/2) alone, which rounded rotations below about 1e-8 rad to zero; composing pi\*n with itself is exact for any axis. With it the implicit Runge-Kutta solvers run with Lie group nodes at all step sizes (LobattoIIIA4 and Radau3 stalled at small steps); their stage Jacobian has the tangent operator of the rotation increment. Simulations with Lie group nodes change at the level of rounding.   - **notes:** DynamicSolverType.TrapezoidalGGL, LobattoIIIA4, LobattoIIIC4GGL and Radau3: the implicit Runge-Kutta solvers for index-3 constraints in the C++ core, run by SolveDynamic; orders 2, 4, 4 and 3, constant steps or the automatic step size (PI controller) with timeIntegration.absoluteTolerance and relativeTolerance; velocity-level constraints at the implicit stages; Lie group nodes at moderate step sizes.

  - description: The analytic inverse kinematics of exudyn.robotics.future (ComputeIK3R, ComputeIKPuma560, ComputeIKUR) took robot dictionaries of standard DH parameters, printed, returned unchecked or NaN rows and was not used. Decided: KinematicChain.InverseKinematicsAnalytic in C++ and Robot.InverseKinematicsAnalytic in Python, the same algorithm on the product of exponentials of the chain (the subproblems of Paden and Kahan), independent of the DH convention, for 3 revolute joints with the axes 2 and 3 parallel, 6 with a spherical wrist (Puma560, KUKA, Staeubli) and 6 of the UR geometry; all solutions, checked by the forward kinematics, the nearest to a reference first; MakeCorkeRobot moved to urdfImport.py and future.py removed.
  - **notes:** exudyn.robotics: KinematicChain.InverseKinematicsAnalytic (C++) and Robot.InverseKinematicsAnalytic (Python) give all solutions of the inverse kinematics of 3R robots and of 6R robots with a spherical wrist (Puma560, KUKA, Staeubli) or of the UR geometry, checked by the forward kinematics and the nearest to qReference first, for any DH convention, base and tool; about 8 us in C++. exudyn.robotics.future is removed; MakeCorkeRobot is in exudyn.robotics.urdfImport.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-05 11:35**, date raised: 2026-11-05
- **1.13.372** `EXTENSION` `HIGH EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` exudyn.cUtilities.KinematicChain: the forward kinematics, the Jacobian and the static torques of a robot in C++ (#3259)
  - description: Robot.LinkHT, JointHT, Jacobian and StaticTorques of exudyn.robotics compute in Python (17, 23 and 114 us for 6 links); the static compensation in a PreStepUserFunction makes a kinematic tree simulation 15 times slower. Decided (design robotics.md, decision 10): a class KinematicChain in exudyn.cUtilities with the link data of Robot (joint types, parents, preHT, localHT, masses, centers of mass, base, tool, gravity) and JointHT, LinkHT, ToolHT, Jacobian of a point of a link and StaticTorques in one backward pass; Robot.GetKinematicChain() creates it; the Python functions of Robot are the Python versions of the same algorithms, cross-referenced; Robot.StaticTorques uses the same O(n) algorithm. The analytic and numerical inverse kinematics follow in the same class.
  - **notes:** exudyn.cUtilities.KinematicChain: the forward kinematics (JointHT, LinkHT, ToolHT), the Jacobian of a point of a link and the static torques of a serial or tree-like robot in C++, about 1 us per call for 6 links; Robot.GetKinematicChain() creates it from a Robot; Robot.StaticTorques computes in one backward pass as the C++ version.

- **1.13.368** `FIX` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` robotics: the tool frame on the last link frame in InverseKinematicsNumerical and CreateKinematicTree, the steps of InterpolateHTs, the Franka Emika Panda made a Robot, the Puma560 inertias physical (#3255)
  - description: InverseKinematicsNumerical put the tool on the joint frame of the last link, while Robot.LinkHT and Robot.Jacobian put it on the link frame (after localHT), so the IK of a pose from LinkHT failed for robots with a last localHT (UR5: 0.079 m); the tool graphics of CreateKinematicTree were on the joint frame as well. InverseKinematicsNumerical.InterpolateHTs took min instead of max of minSteps and the steps by rotation, so SolveSafe never interpolated. models.py: LinkDict2Robot refused dhMode modDHKK, the mode of the Panda, so the Panda could not be made a Robot; the Puma560 inertias of links 0 and 2 violated the triangle inequality of the principal moments. Decided: the tool HT is relative to the frame of the last link (DH convention, as the RTB) also in the IK and the kinematic tree graphics; InterpolateHTs takes the maximum; LinkDict2Robot builds modDHKK robots; ManipulatorPANDA renamed ManipulatorFrankaEmikaPanda (the old name deprecated); the Puma560 inertias adjusted to physical values.
  - **notes:** robotics: the tool HT is relative to the frame of the last link also in InverseKinematicsNumerical and in the tool graphics of CreateKinematicTree (as LinkHT and Jacobian); InverseKinematicsNumerical.InterpolateHTs takes the larger of minSteps and the steps by rotation; LinkDict2Robot builds robots of dhMode modDHKK; the Franka Emika Panda is ManipulatorFrankaEmikaPanda (ManipulatorPANDA deprecated), checked against the RTB 1.5 Panda: its standard DH parameters corrected, the COM of the last link in the flange frame, the tool the Franka hand; the Puma560 inertias of links 0 and 2 physical (the triangle inequality), said in its docstring.

- **1.13.366** `EXTENSION` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` SolveImplicitRungeKutta with ODE1 and data coordinates; the two error estimates of SolveImplicitRungeKutta and SolveTrapezoidalGGL selectable by errorEstimate (#3253)
  - description: SolveImplicitRungeKutta refuses ODE1 and data coordinates. The error estimate of the order of the method from the stages of two steps (\#3250) is in SolveImplicitRungeKutta only; SolveTrapezoidalGGL estimates from the accelerations of one step (and the mean accelerations of three for v). Maintainer: two kinds of estimators in each integrator, switched by a flag - a simple one of one step, inaccurate, and the accurate one, which needs the stage velocities of the previous step (not available in the C++ solvers yet, but resolvable). Decided: the ODE1 coordinates by the same Runge-Kutta method with their stage velocities as unknowns, the data coordinates by the post-Newton step as SolveTrapezoidalGGL; errorEstimate='twoSteps' or 'oneStep' in both solvers.
  - **notes:** SolveImplicitRungeKutta integrates ODE1 coordinates by the same method and data coordinates by the post-Newton step; SolveImplicitRungeKutta and SolveTrapezoidalGGL take errorEstimate='twoSteps' or 'oneStep', the estimate from the stages of the previous and this step or the simple one of one step.

- **1.13.361** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `NORMAL` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Explicit solver with eliminateConstraints: the RK stages do not fix the eliminated coordinates, which makes RK44 first order (#3240)
  - description: CSolverExplicitTimeInt sets the coordinates of CoordinateConstraints to the ground to zero only at the end of a step and in the accelerations of the end; the stage accelerations rk.stageDerivODE2\_t of these coordinates are not zeroed, so the following stages evaluate the forces with the fixed coordinates moved. A chain of three mass points with fixed coordinates (symbolicExplicitConstraintTest.py): RK44 with 500, 5000 and 50000 steps converges with order 1 (differences 4e-5, 4e-6), while SolveExplicit of exudyn.symbolics.solvers, which zeroes them in every stage, gives the converged result with 500 steps. Explicit Euler is not affected. The coordinate is also set to zero regardless of the offset and the factor of the constraint. Decided: zero the stage accelerations and velocities of the eliminated coordinates, and keep the value of the constraint equation, when the explicit solvers are revised in C++ (RG20.5).
  - **notes:** Exudyn's explicit solvers fix the coordinates of CoordinateConstraints to the ground in every stage of the Runge-Kutta methods, to the value of their equation (offset, factor1, user functions) instead of 0: RK44 and DOPRI5 keep their order with eliminated coordinates (RK44 was of order 1), and results of explicit models with such constraints change; a CoordinateConstraint with velocityLevel=True raises with eliminateConstraints.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-04 22:43**, date raised: 2026-11-04
- **1.13.360** `IMPROVEMENT` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` SolveImplicitRungeKutta: an error estimate of the order of the method from the stage values of this and the previous step (#3250)
  - description: The automatic step size of SolveImplicitRungeKutta estimates the error by the embedded trapezoidal solution, of order h^3: the methods take about the steps of the trapezoidal rule, with errors far below the tolerance. Measured against the true local error (a reference of 64 steps from the same start, the step-doubling idea used only as a reference): the trapezoidal rule of one step overestimates the error of LobattoIIIA4 by 1e3 to 7e4, growing as 1/h^2; the quadrature error of the method against the polynomial through the stage velocities of the previous and this step (for Lobatto the fourth difference, Simpson's error h^5/2880 v'''') estimates it with a constant factor of 0.33 to 0.6 for all step sizes, on an oscillator and a pendulum; the same with the stage accelerations only without constraints, as their stage values are of order 2 with constraints. Decided: the estimate of the order of the method from the stages of the previous and this step, the first step by the trapezoidal rule; no extra solve.
  - **notes:** The automatic step size of SolveImplicitRungeKutta estimates the local error with the order of the method, from the stage velocities of the previous and this step (for the Lobatto methods Simpson's error), without an extra solve: 4 to 23 times fewer steps, with local errors of the size of the tolerances.
  - date resolved: **2026-11-04 22:24**, date raised: 2026-11-04

- **1.13.356** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `NORMAL` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` mbs.Reset() and item changes while the renderer runs: no synchronization with the render thread (#3239)
  - description: MainSystem::Reset deletes the items, the sensors and their stored data without stopping or waiting for the renderer; the render thread may be in UpdateGraphicsData, which checks IsSystemConsistent() only at its start, or in the sensor traces, which check nothing, and then reads freed memory. Adding, deleting or modifying items from Python while the renderer runs is the same race, rarer because the items are not freed. SC.Reset() and deleting a SystemContainer are safe: they detach the renderer first, which stops the render loop and joins its thread. Decided: a lock of the system data, taken by Reset and the item changes and by the render thread while it reads the system, or a request to the render thread to finish its frame first; to be analyzed (docs/dev/design/scope.md section 5).
  - **notes:** mbs.Reset(), adding, deleting and modifying items, mbs.Assemble() and setting visualization parameters wait while the render thread reads the system - its graphics, the sensor traces and the scopes -, and the render thread waits for them, by a lock of each system; the main thread computes the user function drawings the render thread asks for while it waits. rendererItemChangesTest.py.

  - description: SolveTrapezoidalGGL estimates the local error of the positions only, by h^2/12 (a1 - a0), and controls the step by the I controller of Exudyn's explicit solvers: at an equal number of steps it was not better than constant steps on a pendulum and a slider crank, and it rejected 5 to 20 % of the steps. Decided: models of changing time scales - a falling chain of 10 elements fixed at one end and starting nearly vertical upwards, which whips, and a contact sphere -, an estimate of the velocity error, and the common step size controller of revision2026c step RG20.8 in Python first (a PI controller).
  - **notes:** The automatic step size of SolveTrapezoidalGGL of exudyn.symbolics.advancedSolvers estimates the local errors of the coordinates, by the difference of the accelerations at both ends of the step, and of the velocities, by the second difference of the mean accelerations of the last three steps, and controls the step by a PI controller, which rejects few steps; a diverging Newton iteration reduces the step. Measured on a bouncing ball, where it needs a tenth of the steps of a constant step size for the same error, and on a chain falling from nearly upright, where the errors of the unstable start grow and a constant step size is better; symbolicTrapezoidalGGLStepSizeTest.py.

  - description: esym.Real('a', 12.) and esym.Real('a', 13.) are two variables of one name: an expression of both reads as one quantity while the computation, which takes the variables, distinguishes them. esym.Function, VariableSet and SymbolicSystem refuse two variables of one name, but esym.Function accepts an input named as a variable of esym.variables it also reads. A global scope of names, each name once, with an exemption, a reset and a switch, would refuse a second variable at its creation. Decided: evaluated first, with options and recommendations in docs/dev/design/symbolicVariableNames.md (revision2026c step RG12.73).
  - **notes:** A named symbolic variable is a variable of a scope: esym.Real(name, value, scope=mbs), esym.Vector and esym.Matrix give the variable of that name in mbs.symbolicVariables, the new scope of the model - a new one, or the one there with the value set; one of another kind or size is replaced -; without scope the one of esym.variables. A symbolic user function reads only its arguments and the variables of mbs.symbolicVariables, at every call; another named variable and a named variable created while recording are refused. mbs.Reset() empties the scope, GetDictionary and SetDictionary keep it. exudyn.special.deprecations.symbolicVariablesWithoutScope restores the variables of no scope for the transition. - **1.13.276** `IMPROVEMENT` `HIGH EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` exudyn.symbolic: the vector and matrix operations as codes of the table of operations, evaluated in the memory of the program instead of by the nodes of the expression graph (#3176)
  - description: Revision2026c step RG12.65.8 of \#3153. SymbolicProgram computes the scalar operations by their codes, but every vector and matrix operation (sums, products with scalars, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products, transposes, components, dot product, norm, vectors and matrices of components) by a virtual call of its node class of the expression graph (Symbolic.h, SymbolicVector.h, SymbolicMatrix.h), whose result lies in a buffer of that node. These operations get codes and cases of the table that read and write the memory of the program - one contiguous array of the values of all slots, with an offset and a size per slot -, so that the nodes only record and the program alone evaluates: a recording can then be evaluated by several threads at once, copied to the GPU and exported without the nodes; leaves and item outputs stay nodes. The rules of their derivatives are in the table already. Results equal to the bit.
  - **notes:** exudyn.symbolic: the operations of vectors and matrices (+, -, \*, @, the transposed product, multiply, T, the vectors and matrices of components, the dot product, NormL2, the components, == and != of vectors) are computed by the table of operations in one array of the program, as the scalar operations, with the same results to the bit; a recording keeps no values in its nodes; GetStatistics counts them as tableOperations.
  - date resolved: **2026-10-31 22:34**, date raised: 2026-10-31

- **1.13.265** `EXTENSION` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` SymbolicSystem: connector and joint Jacobians by the one-pass derivative of one expression per item in the variables of its nodes (#3166)
  - description: Build the generalized forces of a connector, and the constraint equations and reaction forces of a joint, as one expression in the variables of its nodes (q, q\_t of each node), and take their Jacobian by one EvaluateJacobian pass, instead of the chain rule composed by hand in \_ConnectorJacobian and \_JointJacobian (the derivative by the marker states times the marker Jacobians, plus the terms of marker Jacobians depending on q). The variables per node, so the cost grows with the item, not with the system; the columns scattered by ltg. Also the other coordinates an item can depend on: ODE1 coordinates (ObjectConnectorHydraulicActuatorSimple: forces by the pressures y, its ODE1 RHS by q and q\_t), the algebraic coordinates z of a joint (c\_i = z\_i on free axes and for an inactive joint, C\_q^T z and its derivative by q), and data coordinates (\#3158). Small numerical differences to the composed Jacobian and to the C++ items are accepted; the present code kept as the comparison, accuracy and time measured, then decided which stays.
  - **notes:** SymbolicSystem(mbs, itemJacobians='onePass'): the Jacobians of the connectors and joints by one exudyn.symbolic.Function per item in the coordinates of its bodies and nodes, differentiated in one pass per body or node; equal to the chain rule of 'chainRule' (the default) to rounding, faster
  - date resolved: **2026-10-29 23:07**, date raised: 2026-10-29

- **1.13.241** <span class="textred">`BUG`</span> `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` Diff of pow is NaN for a base \<= 0 also with a constant exponent, so x\*\*2 of a negative x has no derivative (#3135)
  - description: ExpressionPower::Diff returns NaN whenever the base is \<= 0, also when the exponent does not depend on the variable, where d(a^b) = b a^(b-1) da is defined; x\*\*2 records as pow, so the tree derivative (Real.Diff, Vector.Diff, EvaluateJacobian with flatEvaluation = False) of any square of a negative value is NaN. Found 2026-10-28 by symbolicOnePassJacobianTest.py (\#3116), whose one pass treats a constant exponent apart.
  - **notes:** exudyn.symbolic: Diff of pow with an exponent that does not depend on the variable is b\*a^(b-1)\*da also for a base \<= 0, so that x\*\*2 of a negative x has a derivative; NaN for a base \<= 0 only where the exponent depends on the variable. The same per column in the one-pass Jacobian.
  - date resolved: **2026-10-28 13:32**, date raised: 2026-10-28

  - description: revision2026c step RG12.58: the vector and matrix expressions of exudyn.symbolic have no derivative (operator\[\]::Diff not implemented), and Diff takes a scalar named variable only, so a recording cannot be differentiated by a component of its vector arguments. - **1.13.129** `IMPROVEMENT` `LOW EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` ObjectUserBody: reuse the results of its position and rotation user functions for the same time, coordinates and local position (#3028)
  - description: Measured 2026-10-18 with userRigidBodyTest.py (500 implicit steps, Python user functions counted): per evaluation of the right-hand side, ObjectUserBody calls positionJacobianUserFunction 5 times, positionUserFunction, rotationMatrixUserFunction and rotationJacobianUserFunction 2 times each - the markers, the loads and the connector on it ask for the same values; with the last two results of each function kept, by time, coordinates and local position, 45 % of the calls remain.   - **notes:** ObjectUserBody reuses the results of its position, position Jacobian, rotation matrix and rotation Jacobian user functions for the same time, coordinates and local position, which the markers, loads and connectors on it ask for several times per evaluation; a rigid user body solves 1.4 times (Python) and 1.6 times (symbolic) faster. A change of a parameter or a new Assemble clears the stored results.
  - date resolved: **2026-10-18 10:05**, date raised: 2026-10-18

- **1.13.48** `EXTENSION` `MEDIUM EFF` `raised by: Claude-JG` `resolved by: Claude-JG` The portable math functions of Exudyn for Python: initial conditions computed with math.sin or numpy differ per platform (#2956)
  - description: The three models left in UnresolvedOnLinux() after \#2954 compute their initial values in Python with math.sin/math.cos (createSphereQuadContact, createSphereTriangleContact: initial velocities 2\*sin(cnt\*pi/3); generalContactCylinderTest: points on a cylinder and RotationMatrixX, i.e. numpy). glibc and the MSVC UCRT round 2\*sin(4\*pi/3) differently by 1 ULP (-0x1.bb67ae8584ca9p+0 vs ...ca8p+0). With sin/cos replaced by float(exu.symbolic.sin(x)) (EM::Sin), Windows and WSL compute bit-identical ODE2 coordinates in all three models (sha256 equal); the only remaining difference is 1 ULP in np.linalg.norm of the test result (numpy 2.4.6 vs 2.2.4, SIMD summation), while sqrt(math.fsum(x\*x)) agrees. Needed: a documented, vectorized way to call EM::Sin, ... from Python (e.g. a small pybind submodule exudyn.math with sin, cos, ... taking float or numpy arrays), used by rigidBodyUtilities (RotationMatrixX, ...) and by test models; and a platform-independent norm for test results.
